summary: This experimental memo describes ways to reduce the delay when a Mobile IPv6 device moves from one access router to another. That delay can cause packet loss, so the protocol helps the device prepare for the move. It was replaced by RFC 5268.

eli5.summary: When you move between rooms, there is a short gap with no signal. This protocol tries to make the switch smooth. It was later replaced by RFC 5268.

questions: how to reduce mobile ipv6 handover delay
subtitle: Reducing delay when a mobile device switches between wireless networks.

tldr.problem: When a Mobile IPv6 device moves from one access router to another, standard procedures for detecting movement, configuring a new address, and updating its location take several seconds, causing packet loss and disrupting real-time applications like voice calls.
tldr.mechanism: The protocol lets a mobile node discover neighboring networks while still connected to its current router, pre-configure a new address, and set up a tunnel before moving. Upon attachment to the new router, the node announces itself and immediately begins receiving packets.
tldr.outcome: This reduces handover latency significantly. RFC 4068 is experimental and was replaced by RFC 5268, which added refinements.

facts.label: RtSolPr retry timeout
facts.value: At least 2 times typical RTT or 100 milliseconds

facts.label: HI retry timeout
facts.value: At least 2 times typical RTT between routers or 100 milliseconds

facts.label: Default tunnel lifetime
facts.value: Small number of seconds or less

today: RFC 4068 is an Experimental specification that has been replaced by RFC 5268, which refines the protocol and addresses operational experiences from deployments.

sections.title: The Handover Latency Problem
sections.content: Mobile IPv6 allows a device (Mobile Node, or MN) to keep its Internet connection when moving from one access router to another. However, three sequential operations add unacceptable delay: movement detection (discovering that the link has changed), address configuration (getting a new IP address valid on the new subnet), and Binding Update (telling the home agent and correspondents about the new address). This combined delay is often enough to drop packets in real-time applications like Voice over IP. This RFC specifies a protocol to reduce this latency by enabling predictive and reactive handover modes.
sections.eli5: When you move, three things have to happen in order: realizing you moved, getting a new address, and telling everyone where you are. This takes too long.

sections.title: Key Concepts: Predictive and Reactive Modes
sections.content: The protocol introduces two operational modes. In predictive mode, the MN sends a Fast Binding Update (FBU) to its previous access router (PAR) while still connected, establishing a tunnel from the old address to a new prospective address. When the MN detaches and connects to the new access router (NAR), it immediately begins receiving packets through the tunnel. In reactive mode, the MN sends the FBU after attaching to the new network. The key innovation is allowing the MN to learn the new router's address and subnet prefix before moving. The Router Solicitation for Proxy Advertisement (RtSolPr) message asks the current router for information about neighboring networks. The Proxy Router Advertisement (PrRtAdv) message supplies this information, including the neighbor router's address and prefix. With this information, the MN can formulate a prospective New Care of Address (NCoA) before changing links.
sections.eli5: Predictive mode means asking about the next network before you go. Reactive mode means asking right after you arrive. Both are faster than waiting to discover the network from scratch.

sections.title: How the Protocol Works
sections.content: The protocol flow has several stages. First, the MN discovers neighboring access points using link-layer methods (e.g., Wi-Fi scanning). It then sends an RtSolPr to learn the IP coordinates of those neighbors. The PAR responds with PrRtAdv messages containing [Access Point ID, Router Info] tuples, including the NAR's link-layer address, IP address, and subnet prefix. Using this information, the MN configures a prospective NCoA and sends an FBU to the PAR, which establishes a tunnel binding PCoA (old address) to NCoA (new address). The PAR acknowledges with a Fast Binding Acknowledgment (FBack) and may consult the NAR using Handover Initiate (HI) and Handover Acknowledge (HAck) messages. Once tunneling is active, the MN disconnects and connects to the NAR. It sends a Fast Neighbor Advertisement (FNA) to announce itself, and the NAR immediately begins forwarding packets through the tunnel. The MN remains in the tunnel until it completes the full Binding Update with its correspondents.
sections.eli5: First, discover neighbors and learn their addresses. Then tell the old router "send my packets to my new address." When you move, tell the new router you arrived. Packets flow through a tunnel until you are fully set up.

sections.title: Address Configuration and Validation
sections.content: The MN proposes a new care of address (NCoA) based on the prefix learned from PrRtAdv. The NAR must verify that this address is not already in use; if it is, the MN receives a Neighbor Advertisement Acknowledgment (NAACK) option suggesting an alternate address. This avoids address conflicts while avoiding the delay of full Duplicate Address Detection (DAD). The protocol supports assigned addressing, where the NAR assigns an address to the MN rather than the MN choosing one. When assigned addressing is used, the PAR includes the address in the FBack, and the MN must use that assigned address instead of its proposed one. If address collisions occur, they are detected during FNA processing, and the NAR indicates rejection by not forwarding packets.
sections.eli5: The new network checks if your proposed address is free. If not, it suggests a different one. The network can also assign you an address automatically.

sections.title: Tunneling and Binding Updates
sections.content: A tunnel is established between the PAR and NAR, carrying packets addressed to the MN's old address (PCoA) to its new address (NCoA). The MN reverse-tunnels packets back to the PAR using the old address as the source, protecting against ingress filtering at edge networks. The PAR then forwards these reverse-tunneled packets to the correspondent nodes. This arrangement continues until the MN completes a full Binding Update with the home agent and any correspondent nodes, establishing direct routes to the new address. The tunnel uses a lifetime specified in the FBU message, typically a few seconds or less. If an MN returns to the PAR before completing binding updates on the NAR, it sends an FBU with lifetime zero to tear down the tunnel and revert to standard Mobile IPv6 procedures.
sections.eli5: The old router forwards your packets to the new router while you complete the move. You send packets back through the old router until everything is set up. When done, the tunnel is removed.

sections.title: Security and Operational Concerns
sections.content: The access routers must have a security association established out-of-band (outside the scope of this protocol). The Handover Initiate and Handover Acknowledge messages MUST be authenticated using the Authentication Header (AH). RtSolPr and PrRtAdv messages SHOULD include authentication. Unsolicited PrRtAdv messages, which can signal a network-initiated handover, allow the network to inform an MN of an impending handover and to buffer packets that arrive before the MN physically connects. The protocol does not address link-layer switching delay; the handover latency reduction applies only to IP layer procedures. Fast and erroneous movement (such as ping-ponging between two networks) can cause signaling overhead; temporary tunnel lifetimes and application-aware rate limits help mitigate this. An MN that moves faster than the signaling can complete risks losing packets; the protocol recommends using standard Mobile IPv6 in such scenarios.
sections.eli5: Routers must trust each other. The protocol adds delays for security checks and address validation. Moving very fast between networks can break things.
